890.title: The ban
890.hook: Antiochus IV outlaws Torah practice and defiles the Temple
890.tomorrow: The mother and seven sons (2 Maccabees 7)
890.howItsDone: Jews remember the persecution under Antiochus at Hanukkah, when the Al HaNissim passage in the prayers recalls a wicked Greek kingdom that tried to make Israel forget the Torah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seventy-two elders in seventy-two rooms, all writing the same words. Your line was something always stays behind in the original. Today, the meeting of two cultures turns into a law against one of them.
screen: `SOMETHING ALWAYS STAYS BEHIND IN THE ORIGINAL.`

segments.voice: The order arrives in writing. The first book of Maccabees says the king, Antiochus, the one surnamed Epiphanes, writes to his whole kingdom that everyone should be one people, and each should give up their own laws. Then letters go to Jerusalem and the towns of Judah, with a list. No more offerings in the Temple. No Sabbaths or festivals. No circumcising sons. Eat what the law forbids. And at the bottom, the penalty: whoever will not obey shall die. Officers are sent to make sure. For a family in a village in Judah, keeping the Sabbath in their own home was now a crime.
screen: `ALL SHOULD BE ONE PEOPLE.` → `A LIST OF WHAT'S FORBIDDEN.` → `THE SABBATH BECOMES A CRIME.`

segments.voice: The book doesn't soften anything. On the Temple altar, the king's men set up what the King James text calls "the abomination of desolation", an idol's altar where the altar of God had stood. Copies of the books of the law are torn to pieces and burned. Women who circumcised their babies are put to death. And the book is honest that this pressure split the people. Many in Israel went along, offered to idols and broke the Sabbath. Many others refused and would not eat what the law forbade, even when refusing meant dying. Both groups were Jews, under the same pressure. This is not a story of good nations and bad nations. It's what happens when a government decides that one way of life has to disappear. The rabbis later had a word for that kind of time: shmad, a time when practicing at all is forbidden. The Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, teaches that in an ordinary time a person may break many commandments to save a life, but when a ruling power decrees against the faith, even a small custom becomes a line not to cross. One teacher's example is as small as changing a shoe strap. Next come a mother and her sons, a priest in a small town who says no, and the holiday that grew out of it all.
screen: `THE ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION.` · `SOME WENT ALONG. SOME REFUSED.` · then, large: `SHMAD: WHEN PRACTICE IS FORBIDDEN.` · `EVEN A SHOE STRAP MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're free to do because of what you believe or where you come from, light a candle, rest on a certain day, or choose no practice at all, and imagine a letter arriving that forbids it. Then let it go, notice that no such letter came, and spare a thought for anyone, of any faith, who did get one. If you pray, use words from your own tradition for them.
The ban. A king's written order outlawing Sabbath, circumcision and Torah, and an idol set on the Temple altar. Today's word.
Your line: freedom to practice. Under that king, it cost some people everything. Day eight hundred ninety, done.

891.title: The mother and seven sons (2 Maccabees 7)
891.hook: a mother encourages her sons to hold fast to their faith under torture
891.howItsDone: Jewish tradition remembers the mother and her seven sons as an example of kiddush ha-shem, sanctifying God's name, and some communities retell their story at Hanukkah and on Tisha b'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ban: a king's letter that made Sabbath, circumcision and Torah a crime. Your line was freedom to practice. Today, one family meets that law face to face.

A mother and seven brothers are brought before the king. The second book of Maccabees, chapter seven, tells it plainly. The order is simple: eat the forbidden meat, and live. One by one, the brothers refuse. The first to speak says: we are ready to die rather than break the laws of our fathers. The text does not hide what follows; one after another, the sons are tortured and killed, each refusing, each speaking a few last words about God, some about a life beyond this one. And one person in the room has to watch every moment. The chapter turns its eyes to her.
screen: `A MOTHER AND SEVEN BROTHERS.` → `EAT, AND LIVE.` → `ONE BY ONE, THEY REFUSE.`

segments.voice: The text calls her marvelous above all, worthy of honorable memory. She sees her sons die in a single day and bears it with good courage because of her hope in the Lord. And she doesn't stay silent. She encourages each of them in the language of their fathers, with words about where life comes from: I don't know how you came to be in my womb. I didn't give you breath and life, or shape your body. The Creator of the world did, and in mercy, he will give you breath and life again. Then the hardest scene. Only the youngest is left. The king promises him riches and friendship if he'll turn, and asks the mother to talk him into it. She agrees to speak. She leans toward her son and, in the family language, says: have pity on me, who carried you nine months and nursed you three years. Look at the heaven and the earth; God made them out of nothing. Don't be afraid. Then the youngest refuses too. And last of all, the mother dies. The rabbis told their own version in the Talmud, tractate Gittin, set in a different time. There, as the mother dies, a heavenly voice calls out a line from the Psalms, in the King James words: "a joyful mother of children." A strange, painful blessing. The story doesn't say she wasn't crushed. It says that in that room, she encouraged them.
screen: `MARVELOUS ABOVE ALL.` · `IN THE LANGUAGE OF THEIR FATHERS.` · `GOD WILL GIVE BREATH AGAIN.` · then, large: `A JOYFUL MOTHER OF CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who raised you or stood beside you and was brave in a hard moment, a hospital, a border, a job lost, a quiet choice nobody else saw, and let them be as they were, not perfect, just brave once. If no one comes, think of a parent in your community, or today's mother. If you pray, use words from your tradition to honor them.

Your line: she encouraged them. She is remembered for her courage, not only her grief. See you tomorrow.

892.title: Mattathias
892.hook: a priest in Modi'in refuses to sacrifice to idols, and the revolt begins
892.howItsDone: At Hanukkah, Jews add the Al HaNissim passage to their prayers, which names Mattathias son of Yohanan, the Hasmonean high priest, and his sons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mother watched seven sons refuse, and spoke courage to every one. Your line was she encouraged them. Today, a priest says no out loud.

Modi'in is a town, not the capital. The first book of Maccabees says a priest named Mattathias lives there with his five sons: John, Simon, Judas who is called Maccabeus, Eleazar and Jonathan. He has been mourning what's happening in Jerusalem, tearing his clothes, putting on sackcloth. Then the king's officers come to make the town sacrifice to idols, and they go straight to him, because he's a leader there. Their offer is friendly: go first, set the example, and you and your sons will be counted among the king's friends, rewarded with silver and gold. Everyone in town is watching.
screen: `A TOWN, NOT THE CAPITAL.` → `A PRIEST AND FIVE SONS.` → `GO FIRST, AND BE THE KING'S FRIEND.`

segments.voice: He answers loudly, so the whole crowd hears: even if every nation in the king's realm obeys and abandons the ways of its ancestors, I and my sons and my brothers will walk in the covenant of our fathers. Then the story turns violent. Another Jew steps up to offer the sacrifice. Mattathias, burning with zeal, kills him at the altar, kills the king's officer too, and pulls the altar down. The book compares him to Phinehas, the zealous priest in Numbers. It's a hard scene, and some readers are uneasy with it; the book offers no apology. Then Mattathias calls through the town for anyone zealous for the law and faithful to the covenant to follow him, and he and his sons flee to the mountains, leaving everything. Some later Hanukkah retellings put an older cry in his mouth, the call Moses made at the golden calf. In the King James words: "Who is on the LORD's side? let him come unto me." In Hebrew, mi la-Adonai elai. Then a turn that's easy to miss. Some of the faithful hide in the wilderness, the enemy attacks them on the Sabbath, and they refuse even to block the caves. They die, the text says, with their families. When Mattathias hears, he and his friends decide: if anyone attacks us on the Sabbath, we will fight back, or we'll all be wiped out. Refusing the king also meant choosing to stay alive, so the covenant would still have people to keep it.
screen: `I AND MY SONS WILL WALK IN THE COVENANT.` · `THE ALTAR PULLED DOWN.` · then, large: `WHO IS ON THE LORD'S SIDE?` · `FIGHTING BACK ON THE SABBATH.`

893.title: Rededication
893.hook: Judah the Maccabee retakes the Temple and rededicates it
893.howItsDone: Jews celebrate Hanukkah for eight nights beginning on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, lighting one more light each night on a hanukkiah, with blessings, and often placing it where it can be seen from outside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mattathias said no out loud in Modi'in. Your line was who is for the lord. Today, his son walks back into the Temple.

Weeds. Mattathias has died, and his son Judas, called Maccabeus, has led the fighters through battle after battle. Now, the first book of Maccabees says, they go up to Mount Zion and find the sanctuary desolate. The altar profaned. The gates burned. The priests' rooms pulled down. Shrubs growing in the courtyards, like in a forest or on a mountainside. The fighters tear their clothes, put ashes on their heads, and fall on their faces. Then they get up: Judas sends men to hold off the enemy in the fortress nearby, and chooses priests to start cleaning.
screen: `SHRUBS IN THE COURTYARDS.` → `THEY TEAR THEIR CLOTHES.` → `THEN THEY START CLEANING.`

segments.voice: The cleaning is careful. The defiled stones are carried out to an unclean place. Then a hard question: what about the old altar, which had been profaned? They pull it down, but they don't throw the stones away. They store them on the Temple mount, the text says, until a prophet should come to show what to do with them. Prophecy had gone quiet, so the question waits on a pile of stones. Then they build a new altar of whole, uncut stones, following the law. New holy vessels. The lampstand brought back in, the lamps lit. Early on the twenty-fifth day of the month Kislev, they offer sacrifice on the new altar, with songs, harps and cymbals, and keep the dedication of the altar for eight days with gladness. Judas and the people decide it will be kept every year, for eight days. That's Hanukkah. The word means dedication, the same Hebrew word the Torah uses when the tabernacle's altar is first anointed. In the King James words: "This was the dedication of the altar." Notice what's not in the first book of Maccabees: a small jar of oil. That story is in the Talmud, tractate Shabbat, which asks: what is Hanukkah? It tells of one jar of pure oil, sealed by the high priest, enough for one day, that burned for eight. Both stories are part of how Jews remember the holiday. One is about rebuilding with your hands. The other is about light that lasted longer than it should.

894.title: The Hasmoneans
894.hook: the rebels became kings, and later rabbis were wary of their power
894.howItsDone: Students of Pirkei Avot learn Hillel's warning, do not trust in yourself until the day of your death, and the Talmud's stories of King Yannai and of Yochanan the high priest are studied in tractates Kiddushin and Berakhot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, weeds in the Temple courtyards, a new altar, eight days of gladness. Your line was rededicate. Today, a harder question: what happens to rebels after they win?

Words on brass. Near the end of the first book of Maccabees, the people of Jerusalem write their thanks on tablets of brass and set them on pillars on Mount Zion, honoring Simon, a son of Mattathias. The book glows about his years: the land had peace, and every man sat under his own vine and fig tree, with no one to make him afraid. So the people make Simon their leader and high priest, with a condition written into the decree: until a faithful prophet should arise. The family of Mattathias, the Hasmoneans, now holds the sword, the Temple and the government. What does that much power do to a family of heroes?
screen: `THANKS WRITTEN ON BRASS.` → `EVERY MAN UNDER HIS FIG TREE.` → `UNTIL A FAITHFUL PROPHET ARISES.`

segments.voice: Years later, in the Talmud, the Hasmonean ruler is King Yannai, and he wears two crowns: the crown of a king and the crown of the high priest. Tractate Kiddushin tells a tense story. Yannai comes home from a victory and throws a feast for the sages of Israel. At the table, one guest stirs him up, telling him the sages resent him. Then an elder named Yehudah ben Gedidyah speaks, with the whole room listening: King Yannai, let the crown of kingship be enough for you. Leave the crown of priesthood to the descendants of Aaron. Yannai, furious, turns on the sages and kills them, and the world is left desolate of Torah until Shimon ben Shetach restores it. Mattathias's sons risked everything so that no king could force his will on the Temple. Their descendants end up as kings the sages feared. Some readers think that's why, when the Talmud asks what Hanukkah is, it answers with a jar of oil and the lights, not a throne. Another passage, in tractate Berakhot, tells of a high priest named Yochanan who served faithfully for many years and changed at the end. The Talmud ties it to Hillel's warning from Pirkei Avot: do not trust in yourself until the day of your death. The power that rescues can become the power that crushes, sometimes within one family.
screen: `TWO CROWNS ON ONE HEAD.` · `LET THE KINGSHIP BE ENOUGH.` · `OIL AND LIGHTS, NOT A THRONE.` · then, large: `DO NOT TRUST IN YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Think of a moment you had a little power, a promotion, being the oldest sibling, being right in an argument, and look honestly, without judging, at how you used it. Then think of one person you admire who now holds power, and wish them the wisdom of Yehudah ben Gedidyah's line: let one crown be enough. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition to stay faithful to who you were.

895.title: Many Judaisms
895.hook: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others argue over law and Temple
895.howItsDone: Jews today belong to different movements and communities, such as Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and others, and study the Second Temple sects through the Mishnah, the Talmud and the writings of Josephus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Yannai wore two crowns, and a sage told him one should be enough. Your line was heroes can change. Today, the arguments in Jerusalem multiply.

One man in Jerusalem wants to find the right way to live, so he tries all of them. That's how the historian Josephus describes his youth. There were, he says, three schools of thought among the Jews: the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Essenes. He went through all three, from the inside. Then, still not satisfied, he went out to the desert to live with a teacher named Bannus, who wore clothes made from what grew on trees, ate only what grew wild, and bathed in cold water day and night. Only after that did he come back to the city and choose. In those days, being Jewish came in more than one shape.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN TRIES ALL THREE.` → `A TEACHER IN THE DESERT.` → `MORE THAN ONE SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Josephus lays out the schools. The Pharisees keep many customs handed down from the fathers that aren't written in the law of Moses, and teach that souls live on after death. The Sadducees hold that only the written laws are binding, and say the soul does not outlive the body; Josephus says they were fewer but included people of high rank. The Essenes live in close communities and share their property, so that no one among them is rich and no one is poor. And Josephus adds a fourth group, followers of Judas the Galilean, who say God alone is their ruler and will call no man master. The Mishnah lets us hear two of these groups argue. In tractate Yadayim, the Sadducees complain to the Pharisees: you say holy scriptures make the hands impure, but the books the Mishnah calls Hamiram don't? Some readers take that word to mean Homer. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai answers, and the debate goes on, round after round. Notice the shape. These aren't people who've lost their faith. They care so much about the Torah and the Temple that they argue about every detail: what counts as Torah, who should run the Temple, what happens after death, how to live. There were many ways to be Jewish, and the Mishnah keeps the Sadducees' complaint in their own words.

896.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
896.hook: scrolls hidden in caves at Qumran, found in modern times
896.howItsDone: A synagogue may keep a genizah for worn-out books and pages that contain God's name, burying or storing them rather than throwing them away, and visitors to the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem can see some of the scrolls on display.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, and a young Josephus trying them all. Your line was many ways then too. Today, some of those voices turn up in a cave.

A stone goes into a dark hole in a cliff, and something inside breaks. That's the story usually told: a shepherd in the hills above the Dead Sea, looking for a stray animal, tosses a rock into a cave and hears pottery crack. Inside are clay jars, and inside the jars, rolled-up scrolls, written in Hebrew and Aramaic. More caves follow, near a place called Qumran, some holding scrolls, some only scraps. They had been sitting in the dark, in a dry desert, the whole time, waiting.
screen: `A STONE INTO A CAVE.` → `CLAY JARS, ROLLED SCROLLS.` → `WAITING IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Keeping writing in clay jars isn't a new idea; the Tanakh itself describes it. In the book of Jeremiah, with Babylon at the gates, the prophet buys a field, and the deed is to be put away. In the King James words: "put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days." A clay jar, so the words last. In the caves near Qumran, scrolls turned up in clay jars too. Among them are copies of books of the Bible, written out by hand. Beside them are writings of a community's own: rules for a community that lived together and shared what it had, hymns, and commentaries reading the prophets as if they spoke about the readers' own day. Some scholars connect that community with the Essenes Josephus described; others see it differently. Nobody knows for certain who hid the scrolls, or exactly why. Maybe for safekeeping in a dangerous time. Maybe as a resting place. Jewish tradition has its own word for that: genizah, a place where worn-out holy writings are put away instead of thrown out. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, tells of Rabban Gamliel the Elder being brought a translation of the book of Job. He had the builder set it under a course of stones: out of use, but not thrown away.

segments.voice: If you can, find a photo of a Dead Sea scroll and just look, not at the captions, but at the lines of letters, the cracks, the dark edges. If you can't, picture a clay jar with a rolled scroll inside and the cave going quiet around it. Stay with the hands that wrote it and carried it into the dark, and if you pray, give thanks in words from your tradition for those who kept the words safe.
Genizah. A place where worn-out holy writings are put away instead of thrown out, the word Jewish tradition uses for scrolls hidden away like those found near Qumran. Today's word.
